h1: Czech dark and amber lagers and how they differ from German ones
title: Czech Dark and Amber Lagers Explained | Craft Beer School
desc: Czech dark and amber lagers explained: how tmavé and polotmavé differ from German dunkel, schwarzbier and Vienna lager in malt, hops and process.
teaser: Czech dark lager is sweeter and softer than German schwarzbier. Czech amber is hoppier than Vienna lager. Here is why.
standfirst: Czech brewing is famous for its golden pale lager, but Czech pubs also pour excellent amber and dark lagers. They look like their German neighbours and taste quite different. Here is what sets them apart.
sections:
Czech beer is traditionally described by colour and by strength in degrees Plato, the original gravity of the wort. Světlé means pale, polotmavé means amber (literally half dark) and tmavé means dark. Within each colour, výčepní beers are lighter, from 8 to 10 degrees. Ležák beers sit at 11 to 12 degrees. Stronger special beers go higher.

The BJCP lists Czech amber lager and Czech dark lager as styles, with roughly 4.4 to 5.8% ABV for each. Our guide to decoction mashing explains the traditional process behind many of them.

Czech dark lager is deep copper to almost black. Its flavour is rich malt: caramel, toffee, toasted bread, sometimes a soft chocolate or coffee note, often with a touch of residual sweetness. Hop bitterness is moderate and Saaz hops add a light spicy aroma. Roast is gentle, never sharp or burnt.

Some versions are almost dessert like in their sweetness. Others are drier and more roasty. A low level of diacetyl, a buttery note, is acceptable in Czech dark lagers in a way it would not be in German ones.

Floor malted dark malts give that soft, bready richness. Our guide to floor malted Bohemian dark malt covers one of the malts brewers use to get there.

Czech amber lager is light amber to copper. It shares the malt richness of the dark style, with caramel and bread crust, but usually shows more hops: spicy, herbal Saaz in both aroma and bitterness. It feels like a bridge between the golden pale lager and the dark one.

Body is medium, carbonation moderate and the finish balanced rather than dry. Like the dark style, it may carry a trace of diacetyl.
How they differ from German dunkel and schwarzbier

Germany has two dark lager styles, covered in our guide to dunkel and schwarzbier.

  • Munich dunkel is built on Munich malt: bready, toasty, nutty, smooth, with low hop character. It is less sweet than many Czech dark lagers and has almost no caramel or roast.
  • Schwarzbier is black, dry and crisp, with light roast and a clean finish. It is lighter and drier than a Czech dark lager and never sweet.

So a Czech dark lager typically sits between the two: sweeter and more caramel led than either, with more hop spice than dunkel.
How Czech amber differs from Vienna lager and Märzen

Vienna lager and Märzen are amber lagers too. Vienna lager is toasty and lightly sweet with low hops. Märzen is fuller and more bready. Czech amber lager usually has more caramel and more hop presence than either. A Vienna lager feels elegant and dry. A Czech amber feels rounder and more bitter, with that recognisable Saaz spice.

Several things push Czech lagers in their direction:

  • Malt. Czech brewers use Moravian or Bohemian malts, sometimes floor malted, plus caramel and dark malts. German dark lagers lean more on Munich malt and dehusked roasted malt.
  • Process. Decoction mashing, where part of the mash is boiled and returned, is still common. It deepens malt flavour and colour.
  • Fermentation. Czech lager strains and a culture that tolerates a little diacetyl give a softer, rounder beer.
  • Hops. Saaz gives a gentle, spicy bitterness rather than a sharp one.

Czech labels often carry a number with a degree sign, such as 10° or 12°. That is the original gravity in degrees Plato, not the alcohol. A 12° beer started with wort of about 12% dissolved solids by weight and usually ends near 5% ABV. A 10° beer is lighter, closer to 4%.

Look also for the words tmavé or tmavý for dark and polotmavé or polotmavý for amber, sometimes alongside ležák for a full strength lager. A label reading tmavý ležák 12° tells you almost everything: dark, full strength lager brewed from a 12 degree wort. Many export labels translate the colour but keep the degree number, so it is worth knowing.

Czech pubs often serve dark and amber lagers fresh from the tank, with a thick, creamy head. Serve them at around 7 to 10 °C, a little warmer than pale lager, so the malt shows. They pair well with roast meats, sausages, mushroom dishes and in India with kosha mangsho, mutton chops or a rich dal makhani.

Few Indian brewpubs pour Czech dark or amber lager, but more are trying. If you find one, taste it next to a dunkel or Vienna lager if the same taproom offers it. The differences in sweetness and hop character are clear once you know what to look for. Building that side by side habit is the fastest way to learn style.
faqs: It is Czech amber lager. The word means half dark. It is malty with caramel and noticeable Saaz hop character.
Is Czech dark lager the same as schwarzbier?
No. Czech dark lager is usually sweeter and more caramel led. Schwarzbier is drier, crisper and lightly roasty.
Why can Czech lagers taste slightly buttery?
Some carry a low level of diacetyl, which is accepted in Czech styles. In German lagers it would count as a fault.
